summary: A revised discussion of the Pcmail workstation-based distributed mail system, updating RFC 984 after comments and more research on interactive clients and non-PC machines. The design might still change, so implementing it was not advised. It replaced RFC 984 and was itself replaced by RFC 1056.

plainLanguage.summary: Your computer is sometimes off, so a central mailbox holds your letters. This is a better-planned version of that idea, though still not final.

subtitle: A distributed mail system for personal computers with central storage and multiple client workstations.

tldr.problem: Personal computers and workstations are resource-limited, sometimes offline, and often owned in multiples by the same user, making it hard to provide unified mail service across many heterogeneous machines.
tldr.mechanism: PCMAIL splits mail service into a central repository that stores messages and maintains global mail state, and multiple clients on different workstations that each keep local copies and synchronize via the Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP), supporting both interactive (always-connected) and batch (offline) modes.
tldr.outcome: PCMAIL provided an architecture for distributed mail on heterogeneous workstations ranging from IBM PCs to Suns, but as a research design still subject to change, it was not widely implemented. RFC 1056 superseded it with updates.

facts.label: Message flags
facts.value: 16 total (8 for repository use, 8 for future)

today: RFC 993 describes an early distributed mail architecture that was not widely adopted. The design explicitly stated that implementation was not advised because it might change. It was superseded by RFC 1056 in 1988. Modern mail systems like IMAP provide similar distributed functionality with a client-server architecture.

sections.title: Problem and Design Motivation
sections.content: RFC 993 presents PCMAIL, a revised design for a distributed mail system serving multiple workstations. The system addresses the practical reality of personal computing in the mid-1980s: users own multiple workstations of varying capabilities (from small IBM PCs with less than one megabyte of RAM and floppy-disk storage to powerful Suns and Microvaxes with substantial disk), some machines are only occasionally connected to a network, and workstations are portable and may be completely offline. PCMAIL's design goal is to provide flexible mail service across this heterogeneous environment, delivering full functionality to resource-rich machines while providing adequate service to resource-poor ones, supporting both always-connected and intermittently-connected machines.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers are weak (like IBM PCs), some are powerful, some are always plugged in, and some are laptops that travel. One mail system needs to work for all of them. PCMAIL figured out how to do this.

sections.title: Repository and Client Architecture
sections.content: PCMAIL divides into two halves. The repository is a central entity running on a powerful computer with large disk storage, permanently connected to the network. It stores all mail, maintains each user's global mail state, accepts incoming mail from the Internet via SMTP, and acts as a DMSP server. The clients run on individual workstations and may be resource-limited. Each user can have multiple clients (at home, at the office, portable), each maintaining a local copy of the user's global mail state. Clients communicate with the repository via DMSP to synchronize local and global states, ensuring that changes made on one client are propagated to others and to the repository. To handle resource-limited machines, messages are split into a small descriptor (typically 100 bytes with summary information like sender, date, subject, size) and the message body. Clients with limited disk space can store descriptors without storing full message bodies, allowing users to see mail summaries even on machines with minimal storage.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the repository as a central post office with a big filing system. Your computer at home is a client. Your computer at work is another client. Both sync with the post office when they connect. If one computer is too small for full messages, it can at least see short summaries.

sections.title: The Distributed Mail System Protocol (DMSP)
sections.content: DMSP is built on top of the Unified Stream Protocol (USP) and provides operations grouped by object type: general operations (send-version, send-message), user operations (login, logout, set-password), client operations (list-clients, create-client, delete-client, reset-client), mailbox operations (list-mailboxes, create-mailbox, delete-mailbox, reset-mailbox, expunge-mailbox), address operations (list-addresses, create-address, delete-address), bulletin board operations (list-bboards, create-bboard, delete-bboard, subscribe-bboard, unsubscribe-bboard, set-first-unread-message-UID), and message operations (get-descriptors, get-changed-descriptors, reset-changed-descriptors, get-message-text, print-message, copy-message, set-flag). All DMSP operations are failure-atomic, guaranteed either to succeed completely or to leave mail state unchanged, so clients can be abruptly disconnected without corruption. Messages can be marked with sixteen flags: eight reserved for the repository (deleted, seen, forwarded-to, forwarded-by, filed, printed, replied-to, copied) and eight for future use.
sections.plainLanguage: DMSP is the language the repository and clients use to talk to each other. It has commands like login, get my mail, send a message, delete a message, create a folder. Every command either completely works or does nothing, so if the connection breaks, nothing gets corrupted.

sections.title: Interactive and Batch Operation Modes
sections.content: PCMAIL supports two operating modes for clients. In interactive mode, used by always-connected clients, changes to the local mail state are immediately transmitted to the repository via DMSP operations. Any incoming mail is immediately transmitted from repository to client. In batch mode, used by intermittently-connected clients, the user manipulates the local mail state locally, queuing changes. When the client next connects to the repository, all queued changes are executed in a batch operation, and the local mail state is synchronized with the repository's global mail state. Synchronization is managed by tracking which clients have seen each change. The repository associates with every global mail state change a list of client objects not yet aware of the change. When a client connects and calls get-changed-descriptors, the repository sends only changes that client has not yet recorded. After the client acknowledges receipt, the change is marked as seen by that client.
sections.plainLanguage: If your computer is always online, changes are instant like email today. If your laptop is offline, you queue up your changes and send them all at once when you reconnect. The repository keeps track of who has seen what so it does not send you old news.

sections.title: Implementation Status and Limitations
sections.content: The RFC describes a current PCMAIL system running at MIT's Laboratory for Computer Science on a VAX-750 under UNIX. The repository is implemented in C on 4.2/4.3BSD UNIX and manages user objects (username, password, client list, mailbox list), mailbox objects (name, message count, unseen count, next UID), client objects (name, status), and message objects (descriptor and body). IBM PC client code operates only in batch mode due to MS-DOS development environment and memory constraints: users manipulate mail via a window-based user interface program, and a separate synchronization program converts queued actions into DMSP operations when the user runs it. UNIX client code runs on Suns, Microvaxes, and VAX-750s in fully interactive mode within GNU-EMACS, with the DMSP implementation built into the EMACS kernel, allowing immediate changes to be reflected in the repository. The RFC notes that PCMAIL works well for small user communities but performance at larger scales was unknown. IBM PC operation is limited by resource constraints and is slow; UNIX clients are far easier to use and faster.
sections.plainLanguage: MIT built PCMAIL and tested it. The central repository ran on a VAX. IBM PC clients worked offline, queuing changes. UNIX clients like Suns could work interactively inside the EMACS editor. It worked well for a small group but no one knew if it would scale.

left.title: Interactive Mode
left.desc: Always connected. Changes are sent immediately and reflected in real time.

right.title: Batch Mode
right.desc: Occasionally connected. Changes are queued and sent in bulk when connected.
